reducing-ozone-depletion-s2.title: A town debates its old refrigerators
reducing-ozone-depletion-s2.html:
CFC production has ended, yet our job is not done. Thousands of refrigerators, freezers and air conditioners made before the 1990s are still in basements and garages across town, each holding a charge of CFC refrigerant. When these machines are crushed at the scrapyard without first draining the refrigerant, the gas escapes into the air and begins its slow trip to the stratosphere. Capturing it costs a few dollars per appliance. Leaving it costs the ozone layer.

endangered-species-s2.title: How the bald eagle came back
endangered-species-s2.html:
In 1963 only 417 nesting pairs of bald eagles were left in the lower 48 states. The pesticide DDT, sprayed widely after World War II, washed into lakes and built up in the fish that eagles eat. In the eagles it caused thin eggshells that broke during nesting. The United States banned DDT for most uses in 1972, and the Endangered Species Act protected the birds and their nesting sites from shooting and disturbance. By 2007 there were 9,789 breeding pairs, and the bald eagle was removed from the endangered and threatened species list.

Summarized from U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, "Bald Eagle Numbers Soaring" (2007): 417 nesting pairs in 1963, 9,789 breeding pairs in 2007, lower 48 states.

human-impacts-biodiversity-s1.title: Habitat fragmentation and a wildlife corridor

human-impacts-biodiversity-s2.title: A village debates clearing its forest
human-impacts-biodiversity-s2.html:
A company has offered to buy the forest above our village and clear it for cattle. The money is tempting. But the forest holds the soil on our hillsides, filters the stream we drink from and keeps our river full of fish. Dozens of birds and orchids found nowhere else live there. Ranch income would last a few decades at most; once the soil washes away, it would end. The forest’s gifts are free, and they would be gone for good.

Invented passage for practice.
